passage: Swati, you asked how it went with my parents, so here it is. I'm Parul, and you know the plan they had: finish B.Com, then CA, then a match from Papa's friends' circle. At Diwali, Mummy brought out a photo of a boy from Indore. Last year I shouted, and it ended with everyone crying and nobody listening. This time I waited until the guests left, made tea for both of them, and said, "I love you, and I know you're thinking of my future. But I'm not ready to meet anyone, and I want to try the design course first." Papa went silent. Mummy said I was being disrespectful, that in her day nobody said no. I said, "I'm not saying no to you. I'm saying not now, and not this." It took three weeks of quiet dinners. Last Sunday Papa asked what the design course involves. That's his way of saying maybe.

qa.q: Where was the boy in the photo from?
qa.a: Indore.

qa.q: What does Parul waiting for the guests to leave and making tea suggest about how Parul felt?
qa.a: Parul was nervous but determined, and caring too, wanting to refuse without hurting them after last year's shouting match.

qa.q: What made this refusal work better than last year's?
qa.a: A calm moment, warm words, separating "not now, not this" from rejecting them, and giving them time.

qa.q: How did Mummy see Parul's refusal?
qa.a: As disrespect, since in her day nobody said no to parents, so she likely felt hurt and challenged.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult setting limits on family expectations about career and marriage with calm, warm explanation and time rather than confrontation.

subtype: Making commitments to study, work and partners [Expressing]
passage:
Gargi: the landlord wants us to sign the 11-month lease by friday!! the flat with the balcony 😍
Dolma: I love it too. but before I say yes, can we check a few things?
Gargi: like what
Dolma: my internship might move me to Pune in March. if that happens, can I sublet, or am I stuck?
Gargi: hmm. didn't think of that
Dolma: also who pays if the geyser breaks. and is the deposit returned
Gargi: you sound like my dad 😅
Dolma: haha. I just don't want to promise you 11 months and then leave you stranded
Gargi: okay that's actually sweet. I'll ask the landlord tonight
(later)
Gargi: subletting is fine with a month's notice. he'll write it into the lease
Dolma: then I'm in. properly in 🤝

qa.q: How long is the lease?
qa.a: Eleven months.

qa.q: Why did Dolma want to check things before saying yes?
qa.a: Dolma loved the flat too but felt worried about breaking a promise to Gargi if the internship moved to Pune in March.

qa.q: What made Dolma's final yes more reliable?
qa.a: Checking the terms and Dolma's own situation first, and getting the subletting clause written into the lease.

qa.q: How did Gargi come to see Dolma's questions?
qa.a: First as fussy, "like my dad", then as caring, since Dolma didn't want to leave Gargi stranded.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult making a costly commitment like a lease only after checking the terms and their own capacity, to avoid a broken promise.

passage: The rain hadn't stopped for three days, and Chaitanya's scraped arm was still bandaged when Imran knocked with a steel tiffin of dal-chawal and the week's lecture notes. He had come every evening since the skid, missing his own cricket practice. Tonight Chaitanya pushed the notes aside. "Just don't tell anyone how it happened. Especially not my parents." Imran sat on the edge of the bed. He knew how it happened: two beers at Nikhil's party, then the bike on a wet road. "I'll bring food as long as your arm needs it. I'll copy every note," he said. "But I'm not keeping quiet if you ride after drinking again. That's not loyalty. That's watching you get hurt." Chaitanya stared at the rain. "You'd really tell?" "I'd tell. And I'm keeping your keys till the exams are over." He held out his hand. After a long moment, Chaitanya dropped the keys into it.

qa.q: What did Imran bring when he knocked?
qa.a: A steel tiffin of dal-chawal and the week's lecture notes.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when Chaitanya asked for silence?
qa.a: Imran felt torn: loyal and caring, but worried that staying quiet would mean watching Chaitanya get hurt again.

qa.q: How did Imran combine loyalty with honesty?
qa.a: He kept caring in practical ways, with food, notes and time, while refusing to stay silent about riding after drinking and taking the keys until the exams.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have felt handing over the keys?
qa.a: Probably ashamed and a little cornered, but also cared for, since Imran's daily help showed the demand came from love.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult showing care through time, help and follow-through, and a loyalty that allows honesty instead of silence about harm.

passage: So, you asked on the podcast about the best congratulations I ever gave. I'm Madhuri, and honestly I learnt it by getting it wrong first. When my flatmate Jahnavi got her job offer from the Chennai firm, I burst into her room with a party popper and a speaker blasting dance music. She smiled, but it was a thin smile. She said thanks and went back to her laptop. Later I saw her on the balcony, very quiet. The job meant leaving her mother alone in Nagpur, and she was proud and sad at the same time. My confetti had drowned all of that. The next morning I left a note on her chai mug: "You earned this with every late night I watched you work. I'm proud of you, and I'm here for the hard parts too." She came to find me with the note in her hand and hugged me for a long time. That was the real congratulations.

qa.q: Where was Jahnavi's job offer from?
qa.a: The Chennai firm.

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel on seeing Jahnavi quiet on the balcony?
qa.a: Madhuri felt a pang of regret, sensing that the loud celebration had drowned out Jahnavi's mixed feelings.

qa.q: What made the note work better than the party popper?
qa.a: It was brief, specific about Jahnavi's effort and made room for both pride and sadness, matching her mood instead of performing cheer.

qa.q: What was the party popper moment like for Jahnavi?
qa.a: Proud but sad about leaving her mother, Jahnavi probably felt the loud cheer didn't fit her mood, so she gave a thin smile and withdrew.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult learning to match congratulations to a friend's mood, where a brief, specific note of pride feels more sincere than overdone cheer.

subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and at the end of my final-year project I didn't know how to thank Professor Mridul Bora. He had read four drafts, stayed late when our sensor failed, and never once made me feel stupid. On Teachers' Day some classmates had touched his feet and given him a shawl; he'd accepted with a slightly embarrassed smile. Back home in Aizawl we'd more likely cook for a teacher or bring a small gift, and touching feet isn't our custom; it didn't feel like mine to borrow. So I did two things. At the final presentation, on the first slide, I wrote, "Thanks to Prof. Mridul Bora, whose questions made this better." And I left a handwritten note on his desk saying which of his questions had changed my design. A week later he stopped me in the corridor. "That note," he said. "It's in my drawer." He looked more pleased than he had with the shawl.

qa.q: What did some classmates give the professor on Teachers' Day?
qa.a: A shawl, and they touched his feet.

qa.q: Why was Lalremsiami unsure how to thank the professor?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt deeply grateful but uncertain, since touching feet wasn't Lalremsiami's custom and borrowing it didn't feel genuine.

qa.q: Which forms of thanks suited Lalremsiami best?
qa.a: A public acknowledgement on the first slide and a handwritten note naming the question that changed the design: specific, timely and sincere.

qa.q: How did Professor Bora seem to receive the note?
qa.a: He was clearly touched, keeping it in his drawer and seeming more pleased than he had been with the shawl.

grounding: It illustrates a student thanking a mentor with a note and a timely acknowledgement, while showing that customs of respect such as touching feet or gifts differ.

passage:
Tuesday: When the news came that Urmila's father had died in Jaipur, the class group filled with long messages: "everything happens for a reason", "he's in a better place". Gargi deleted three drafts before sending one line: "Urmila, I'm so sorry. I'm here, whenever." Urmila replied with a single heart.
The following Monday: Urmila was back at the hostel, pale and quiet. Gargi didn't quiz her. She left a steel box of poha outside Urmila's door and a folder of the lab notes she'd missed, with a sticky note: "No need to reply."
Three weeks later: The class had moved on to exam talk. Gargi texted, "Thinking of you today. Want to walk to the tea stall?" Urmila wrote back, "Yes. Everyone else stopped asking." On the walk she talked for twenty minutes about her father's terrible jokes, and laughed once.

qa.q: What did Gargi leave outside Urmila's door?
qa.a: A steel box of poha and a folder of the lab notes she'd missed.

qa.q: Why did Gargi delete three drafts before sending one line?
qa.a: Gargi felt anxious about saying the wrong thing and uneasy with the clichés filling the group, and wanted something short and sincere.

qa.q: What made Gargi's support helpful over time?
qa.a: A simple, sincere message, practical help with no pressure to reply, and a follow-up weeks later when others had stopped asking.

qa.q: What was it like for Urmila three weeks after the loss?
qa.a: She felt others had moved on, since "everyone else stopped asking", so Gargi's invitation let her talk about her father and even laugh.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult offering condolences with a short sincere message, quiet practical help and a later follow-up instead of clichés.

passage: Sit, Rashmi. You asked why I didn't rush to Mrs Wadia's house with food when her husband died. Let me tell you something from when I was twenty-one, in the girls' hostel in Pune. My roommate Dinaz lost her mother in the winter term. In our Marathi home, when someone died, the whole neighbourhood arrived: pots of food, aunties on the floor, nobody left alone for a minute. So I gathered six girls with tiffins and we marched to Dinaz's family flat. Her aunt opened the door, thanked us very politely, took the food, and did not invite us in. I was hurt. Later Dinaz told me her family preferred to grieve quietly in the first days; the food had helped, but a crowd would not have. After that I learnt to ask the family first, or send food with a note and wait. That's why, this morning, your Irawati Aaji phoned Mrs Wadia's daughter before doing anything.

qa.q: How old was Irawati Aaji when Dinaz lost her mother?
qa.a: Twenty-one.

qa.q: How did young Irawati feel when Dinaz's aunt took the food but didn't invite them in?
qa.a: She felt hurt, because in her own family a crowd of visitors was how love and support were shown.

qa.q: What did young Irawati learn to do differently after that visit?
qa.a: To ask the family first, or to send food with a note and wait, following the family's lead.

qa.q: How might Dinaz's family have experienced six girls arriving with tiffins?
qa.a: The food was welcome, but a crowd at the door would have intruded on their wish to grieve quietly in the first days.

grounding: It illustrates that consolation differs across cultures, with some bringing food and visiting in groups and others preferring privacy, so the helper follows the family's lead.

passage:
Thursday night
Today was strange but good. Yesterday Hansa ma'am snapped at me in front of the whole team over a formatting mistake that wasn't even mine. I went home furious and rehearsed what I'd say when she apologised. She never said sorry. Instead, this morning she put a cup of filter coffee on my desk, made exactly the way I take it, and asked me to lead the client call. At lunch she waved me over to her table, and that was that. Back to normal, as if a door had been quietly closed.
My flatmate Keiko says that counts as a full apology; at her home, a shared meal after a fight says more than any words. Part of me still wanted the actual sentence. Mumma apologises the same way as Hansa ma'am, with food, and Papa with folded hands and a joke. Maybe I'm the only one in my family who needs the words. One day I might tell ma'am that.
Damini

qa.q: What did Hansa ma'am put on Damini's desk?
qa.a: A cup of filter coffee, made exactly the way Damini takes it.

qa.q: How did Damini feel about Hansa ma'am's way of making up?
qa.a: Damini felt mixed: relieved and a little touched that things were back to normal, but part of Damini still wanted to hear an actual sorry.

qa.q: What could Damini do if the spoken words still matter?
qa.a: Tell Hansa ma'am calmly, at a good moment, that spoken apologies matter, while still treating the coffee, the call and the lunch as real repair.

qa.q: How does Keiko see what Hansa ma'am did?
qa.a: As a full apology, since in her home a shared meal after a fight says more than words.

grounding: It illustrates that apology norms vary, with some people expecting explicit words and others repairing through a gift, a shared meal or a return to routine.

passage:
Sunday: Two days after the party, Jasleen typed and deleted for an hour, then sent: "I told everyone about your crush on Kunal and turned it into a joke. That was my fault, and I'm sorry. You don't have to reply." No reply came. Jasleen checked her phone every ten minutes, then made herself stop.
Thursday: Reena passed her in the library and gave a small nod, nothing more. Jasleen's stomach dropped, but she didn't chase after her. That night a message arrived: "Got your text. I'm still angry. Need some time." Jasleen answered: "Okay. I'll be here when you're ready."
Two weeks later: Reena sat down across from her at the canteen. "It wasn't just the crush," she said. "It felt like my secrets were entertainment." Jasleen didn't defend herself. She listened, then said, "You're right. I wanted the laugh more than I protected you." Reena pushed half her samosa across the table.

qa.q: What did Jasleen reveal at the party?
qa.a: Reena's crush on Kunal.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel while waiting for a reply?
qa.a: Jasleen felt anxious and guilty, checking the phone every ten minutes but making herself stop so as not to pressure Reena.

qa.q: What helped repair the friendship?
qa.a: Jasleen named her own part without excuses, didn't demand forgiveness, gave Reena time, and listened without defending herself.

qa.q: What was the rupture like for Reena?
qa.a: It felt as if her secrets were entertainment, so she stayed angry and needed two weeks before she could talk.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult repairing a friendship by naming their part, giving the other person days of space, and listening without demanding forgiveness.

passage: I share the flat with Jatin, so I was on the sofa when Sarita came round on Friday with plans for the new café and a big grin. Jatin had been quiet all evening after a long shift at the hospital pharmacy; he'd eaten standing up and gone to his room. When she called him out and told him the plan, he rubbed his face and said calmly, "I'm really glad you thought of it. But I need some time alone tonight. Can we go tomorrow instead?" There was a pause. Sarita's grin slipped for a second, and I braced for a sulk; my last flatmate would have hinted for an hour and then slammed a door. But she said, "Okay. Tomorrow, seven?" and he said, "Seven. I'd like that." She left and he went back to his room. I can't say exactly how either of them felt. But the next evening they went out laughing, and nobody had to guess anything.

qa.q: Where had Jatin worked his long shift?
qa.a: At the hospital pharmacy.

qa.q: What do Jatin's quiet evening and rubbed face suggest about his state?
qa.a: He was likely tired and drained after the long shift and needed rest more than an outing, though he still seemed glad Sarita had thought of him.

qa.q: Why did Jatin's way of saying it work?
qa.a: He stated a clear, calm, specific need, thanked her, and offered another time, so Sarita didn't have to guess.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Sarita?
qa.a: She was briefly disappointed, her grin slipping, but the clear request made it easy to agree to seven the next day.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using a calm "I need" statement to ask for time alone, which is easier to honour than hints.
